claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) latently infects roughly one-third of the world's population.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), latently infects roughly one-third of the world's population and causes 1–2 million deaths per year.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction, representing established knowledge about TB prevalence.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes 1–2 million deaths per year.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), latently infects roughly one-third of the world's population and causes 1–2 million deaths per year.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction, representing established knowledge about TB mortality.

claim: Tuberculous cervical lymphadenopathy (scrofula) represents 10% of all new cases of TB.
source: For example, a disease known as tuberculous cervical lymphadenopathy, or scrofula, represents 10% of all new cases of TB, and frequently manifests without lung involvement (Fontanilla et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fontanilla et al., 2011.

claim: Tuberculous cervical lymphadenopathy frequently manifests without lung involvement.
source: For example, a disease known as tuberculous cervical lymphadenopathy, or scrofula, represents 10% of all new cases of TB, and frequently manifests without lung involvement (Fontanilla et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fontanilla et al., 2011.

claim: The oropharynx and upper airway lymphatics drain to the cervical lymph nodes.
source: Because the oropharynx and upper airway lymphatics drain to the cervical lymph nodes, while the lower airway lymphatics drain to the mediastinal lymph nodes, infection of the cervical lymph nodes by Mtb may not involve the lower airways.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical knowledge about lymphatic drainage patterns.

claim: The lower airway lymphatics drain to the mediastinal lymph nodes.
source: Because the oropharynx and upper airway lymphatics drain to the cervical lymph nodes, while the lower airway lymphatics drain to the mediastinal lymph nodes, infection of the cervical lymph nodes by Mtb may not involve the lower airways.
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical knowledge about lymphatic drainage patterns.

claim: Infection of the cervical lymph nodes by Mtb may not involve the lower airways.
source: Because the oropharynx and upper airway lymphatics drain to the cervical lymph nodes, while the lower airway lymphatics drain to the mediastinal lymph nodes, infection of the cervical lymph nodes by Mtb may not involve the lower airways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical knowledge of lymphatic drainage patterns.

claim: In the Lübeck Disaster, the majority of infected infants and children developed lymphatic and oropharyngeal TB rather than pulmonary TB.
source: Indeed, in the infamous 'Lübeck Disaster' where hundreds of infants and children were accidentally orally administered Mtb instead of the attenuated BCG vaccine, the majority developed lymphatic and oropharyngeal TB rather than pulmonary TB (Fox et al., 2016), highlighting how inoculation via the oropharyngeal route can cause extrapulmonary disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fox et al., 2016.

claim: Inoculation via the oropharyngeal route can cause extrapulmonary disease.
source: Indeed, in the infamous 'Lübeck Disaster' where hundreds of infants and children were accidentally orally administered Mtb instead of the attenuated BCG vaccine, the majority developed lymphatic and oropharyngeal TB rather than pulmonary TB (Fox et al., 2016), highlighting how inoculation via the oropharyngeal route can cause extrapulmonary disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Lübeck Disaster case, supported by citation to Fox et al., 2016.

claim: Microfold cells (M cells) overlie the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).
source: Specialized epithelial cells known as microfold cells (M cells) overlie the MALT and are able to translocate luminal material to basolateral antigen-presenting cells located immediately beneath the M cell (Kimura, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimura, 2018.

claim: M cells are able to translocate luminal material to basolateral antigen-presenting cells located immediately beneath the M cell.
source: Specialized epithelial cells known as microfold cells (M cells) overlie the MALT and are able to translocate luminal material to basolateral antigen-presenting cells located immediately beneath the M cell (Kimura, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimura, 2018.

claim: M cells can initiate an immune response to pathogens or material found within the lumen.
source: In this way, M cells can initiate an immune response to pathogens or material found within the lumen (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: M cells have been found in the upper and lower airways of both mice and humans.
source: Within the respiratory tract, M cells have been found in the upper and lower airways of both mice and humans (Fujimura, 2000; Kim et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujimura, 2000; Kim et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2019.

claim: M cells express a number of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).
source: M cells express a number of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) (Mabbott et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mabbott et al., 2013.

claim: The cellular prion protein (PrP(C)) is a receptor for Brucella abortus.
source: For example, the cellular prion protein (PrP(C)), a receptor for Brucella abortus, is necessary for B. abortus translocation (Nakato et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakato et al., 2012.

claim: The cellular prion protein (PrP(C)) is necessary for B. abortus translocation.
source: For example, the cellular prion protein (PrP(C)), a receptor for Brucella abortus, is necessary for B. abortus translocation (Nakato et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakato et al., 2012.

claim: Glycoprotein 2 (GP2) expressed on the apical surface of gastrointestinal M cells recognizes FimH.
source: Similarly, glycoprotein 2 (GP2) expressed on the apical surface of gastrointestinal M cells recognizes FimH, a component of the type I pili found on both commensal and pathogenic bacteria (Hase et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hase et al., 2009.

claim: FimH is a component of the type I pili found on both commensal and pathogenic bacteria.
source: Similarly, glycoprotein 2 (GP2) expressed on the apical surface of gastrointestinal M cells recognizes FimH, a component of the type I pili found on both commensal and pathogenic bacteria (Hase et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hase et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of either the host receptor GP2 or the bacterial ligand FimH diminishes bacterial translocation through M cells.
source: Loss of either the host receptor GP2 or the bacterial ligand FimH diminishes bacterial translocation through M cells, reducing the immune response to these antigens and bacteria within Peyer's patches (Hase et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hase et al., 2009.

claim: Mtb uses airway M cells as a portal of entry to initiate infection.
source: We previously demonstrated that Mtb uses airway M cells as a portal of entry to initiate infection (Nair et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work, Nair et al., 2016.

claim: The Mtb type VII secretion system is required for bacterial binding to M cells in vitro.
source: To test if the Mtb T7SS was necessary for M cell binding, we incubated transwells with either wild-type Mtb expressing mCherry (WT Mtb) or Mtb eccD1::Tn expressing mCherry at 4°C to prevent bacterial entry or translocation and analyzed surface binding by confocal microscopy and quantification of colony-forming units (CFU) (Figure 1C–E). Consistent with our prior data (Nair et al., 2016), significantly more WT Mtb bound HBE/Raji B transwells (containing M cells) than control transwells by both microscopy (Figure 1C,D) and CFU (Figure 1E). However, binding was greatly reduced for the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E, demonstrating reduced binding of the T7SS mutant strain.

claim: Significantly more WT Mtb bound HBE/Raji B transwells (containing M cells) than control transwells.
source: Consistent with our prior data (Nair et al., 2016), significantly more WT Mtb bound HBE/Raji B transwells (containing M cells) than control transwells by both microscopy (Figure 1C,D) and CFU (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and citation to prior work.

claim: Binding was greatly reduced for the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain compared to WT Mtb.
source: However, binding was greatly reduced for the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: No significant insertions, deletions or mutations were observed in the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain relative to the wild-type strain.
source: No significant insertions, deletions or mutations were observed in the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain relative to the wild-type strain, although several single-nucleotide polymorphisms were noted when we compared the strains to the reference strain (Miyoshi-Akiyama et al., 2012; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The Mtb T7SS is necessary to facilitate mycobacterial translocation across M cells.
source: To test if the Mtb T7SS is necessary to facilitate mycobacterial translocation across M cells, we infected the apical chamber of transwells with either WT Mtb or Mtb eccD1::Tn and measured translocation to the basal compartment. As we reported previously (Nair et al., 2016), WT Mtb translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells to a greater extent than control transwells, while the translocation of the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain was significantly reduced (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: WT Mtb translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells to a greater extent than control transwells.
source: As we reported previously (Nair et al., 2016), WT Mtb translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells to a greater extent than control transwells, while the translocation of the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain was significantly reduced (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and citation to prior work.

claim: The translocation of the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain was significantly reduced compared to WT Mtb.
source: As we reported previously (Nair et al., 2016), WT Mtb translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells to a greater extent than control transwells, while the translocation of the Mtb eccD1::Tn strain was significantly reduced (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) was stable during the translocation experiment.
source: Importantly, the transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), a measure of epithelial monolayer integrity (Srinivasan et al., 2015), was stable during the experiment (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mtb translocated across Caco-2/Raji B transwells in a T7SS-dependent manner.
source: Similar to HBE/Raji B transwells, we observed that Mtb translocated across Caco-2/Raji B transwells in a T7SS-dependent manner (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H,I.

claim: EsxA-beads translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells without disrupting the epithelial monolayer.
source: EsxA-beads but not control beads translocated across HBE/Raji B transwells (Figure 2A) without disrupting the epithelial monolayer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: EsxA-beads, but not EsxB-beads or control beads, translocated across Caco-2/Raji B transwells.
source: EsxA-beads, but not EsxB-beads or control beads, also translocated across Caco-2/Raji B transwells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EsxA directly binds to M cells on HBE/Raji B transwells.
source: We detected robust EsxA binding to M cells on HBE/Raji B transwells, in contrast to EsxB, which did not demonstrate significant binding (Figure 2D,G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, G-H.

claim: EsxB did not demonstrate significant binding to M cells.
source: We detected robust EsxA binding to M cells on HBE/Raji B transwells, in contrast to EsxB, which did not demonstrate significant binding (Figure 2D,G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, G-H.

claim: EsxA, but not EsxB, directly binds the M cell surface and is sufficient to mediate translocation across M cells when conjugated to inert beads.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that EsxA, but not EsxB, directly binds the M cell surface and is sufficient to mediate translocation across M cells when conjugated to inert beads.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: The interaction between transferrin (TRFE) and the transferrin receptor (TFR1) was identified using the TriCEPS reagent system.
source: Using this approach, we identified the interaction between transferrin (TRFE) and the transferrin receptor (TFR1) (Figure 3A, blue peptides; Supplementary file 2), proving the validity of this system.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Peptides for apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and scavenger receptor class B type I (SR-B1) were enriched when cells were treated with EsxA.
source: When cells were treated with EsxA, peptides for two proteins, apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and scavenger receptor class B type I (SR-B1) were enriched (Figure 3A, red peptides; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: SR-B1 is a cell surface molecule.
source: Because ApoE is a soluble protein (Huang and Mahley, 2014) while SR-B1 is a known cell surface molecule, we focused on SR-B1.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and citation.

claim: Western blotting with an anti-SR-B1 antibody detected an approximately 82 kD band consistent with the known observed molecular weight of glycosylated SR-B1.
source: After incubation with biotinylated EsxA, completion of the biotin transfer assay, and subsequent immunoprecipitation with streptavidin-coated beads, western blotting with an anti-SR-B1 antibody detected an approximately 82 kD band consistent with the known observed molecular weight of glycosylated SR-B1 (Acton et al., 1996; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Acton et al., 1996.

claim: SR-B1 expression was higher on HBE/Raji B transwells compared to control transwells.
source: While there was no difference in the number of nuclei per field on the transwells (Figure 3C), SR-B1 expression was higher on HBE/Raji B transwells (Figure 3C,E) and the majority of the SR-B1 positive cells were NKM+ M cells (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3E.

claim: The majority of the SR-B1 positive cells were NKM+ M cells.
source: While there was no difference in the number of nuclei per field on the transwells (Figure 3C), SR-B1 expression was higher on HBE/Raji B transwells (Figure 3C,E) and the majority of the SR-B1 positive cells were NKM+ M cells (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3F.

claim: SR-B1 is a candidate EsxA receptor expressed on M cells in vitro.
source: Taken together, we identify SR-B1 as a candidate EsxA receptor expressed on M cells in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: HBE cells transduced with SR-B1 shRNA showed a robust knock-down of SR-B1 compared to NT shRNA.
source: We first transduced HBE cells with non-targeting (NT) or SR-B1 shRNA and observed a robust knock-down of SR-B1 in HBE cells transduced with the SR-B1 shRNA as compared to the NT shRNA (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HBE/Raji B transwells constructed from NT and SR-B1 shRNA cells had a similar number of M cells.
source: HBE/Raji B transwells constructed from these cells had a similar number of M cells comparing NT and SR-B1 shRNA transwells (Figure 4B,C) and SR-B1 shRNA transwells showed a reduction in SR-B1 expression by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: SR-B1 shRNA transwells showed a reduction in SR-B1 expression by immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: HBE/Raji B transwells constructed from these cells had a similar number of M cells comparing NT and SR-B1 shRNA transwells (Figure 4B,C) and SR-B1 shRNA transwells showed a reduction in SR-B1 expression by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Absence of SR-B1 reduced the number of EsxA positive cells on HBE/Raji B SR-B1 shRNA transwells.
source: When we incubated these transwells with recombinant EsxA, absence of SR-B1 reduced the number of EsxA positive cells on HBE/Raji B SR-B1 shRNA transwells (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4E.

claim: The majority of EsxA-positive cells were SR-B1 positive in HBE/RajiB NT shRNA transwells.
source: Additionally in HBE/RajiB NT shRNA transwells, the majority of EsxA-positive cells were SR-B1 positive (Figure 4B,F), suggesting that EsxA preferentially bound SR-B1 expressing M cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4F.

claim: EsxA preferentially bound SR-B1 expressing M cells.
source: Additionally in HBE/RajiB NT shRNA transwells, the majority of EsxA-positive cells were SR-B1 positive (Figure 4B,F), suggesting that EsxA preferentially bound SR-B1 expressing M cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4F.

claim: SR-B1 is necessary for EsxA binding to M cells.
source: Taken together, we identify SR-B1 as necessary for EsxA binding to M cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data from Figure 4.

claim: Loss of SR-B1 greatly reduced the number of bacteria bound to the HBE/Raji B transwells.
source: Loss of SR-B1 greatly reduced the number of bacteria bound to the HBE/Raji B transwells as determined by confocal microscopy (Figure 4G,H) and by quantification of CFU (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Loss of SR-B1 greatly reduced Mtb translocation in the HBE/Raji B transwells at 37°C.
source: As expected from the reduced bacterial binding (Figure 4G–I), loss of SR-B1 also greatly reduced Mtb translocation in the HBE/Raji B transwells at 37°C (Figure 4J) with no impact on the TEER (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Loss of SR-B1 had no impact on the TEER during Mtb translocation experiments.
source: As expected from the reduced bacterial binding (Figure 4G–I), loss of SR-B1 also greatly reduced Mtb translocation in the HBE/Raji B transwells at 37°C (Figure 4J) with no impact on the TEER (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa was able to translocate equally across NT and SR-B1 shRNA HBE/Raji B transwells.
source: The reduced ability of Mtb to translocate across HBE/Raji B transwells expressing SR-B1 shRNA was not due to any intrinsic defect in translocation caused by SR-B1 deficiency as another airway pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, was able to translocate equally across NT and SR-B1 shRNA HBE/Raji B transwells (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: P. aeruginosa does not encode a T7SS or EsxA homologue.
source: Of note, P. aeruginosa does not encode a T7SS or EsxA homologue, suggesting that its translocation across M cells depends on unique bacterial and host factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about P. aeruginosa genetics.

claim: P. aeruginosa translocation across M cells depends on unique bacterial and host factors.
source: Of note, P. aeruginosa does not encode a T7SS or EsxA homologue, suggesting that its translocation across M cells depends on unique bacterial and host factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that P. aeruginosa lacks T7SS and EsxA but can still translocate.

claim: SR-B1 is essential for the binding and translocation of Mtb via M cells in a process requiring the effector EsxA.
source: We thus conclude that SR-B1 is essential for the binding and translocation of Mtb via M cells in a process requiring the effector EsxA.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data from Figure 4.

claim: M cells are found in the upper and lower airways of mice and humans.
source: M cells are found in the upper and lower airways of mice and humans (Fujimura, 2000; Mutoh et al., 2016; Nair et al., 2016; Teitelbaum et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujimura, 2000; Mutoh et al., 2016; Nair et al., 2016; Teitelbaum et al., 1999.

claim: Mouse nasal-associated lymphoid tissue (NALT) demonstrated robust SR-B1 staining on the surface of NKM 16-2-4 positive cells.
source: Mouse nasal-associated lymphoid tissue (NALT), a region enriched for M cells (Mutoh et al., 2016; Nair et al., 2016; Park et al., 2003), demonstrated robust SR-B1 staining on the surface of NKM 16-2-4 positive cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SR-B1+/NKM 16-2-4- cells were not observed in NALT epithelia in vivo.
source: Importantly, we did not observe SR-B1+/NKM 16-2-4- cells, demonstrating that SR-B1 is specific for M cells in the NALT epithelia in vivo.
evidence: This is based on the absence of observation in the experimental data from Figure 5A.

claim: SR-B1 is specific for M cells in the NALT epithelia in vivo.
source: Importantly, we did not observe SR-B1+/NKM 16-2-4- cells, demonstrating that SR-B1 is specific for M cells in the NALT epithelia in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of SR-B1+/NKM- cells in the experimental data.

claim: Both the Mtb eccD1::Tn and Mtb∆esxA strains had 1.0–1.5 log fewer bacteria compared to WT Mtb in the cervical lymph nodes.
source: Both the Mtb eccD1::Tn and Mtb∆esxA strains had 1.0–1.5 log fewer bacteria compared to WT Mtb in the cervical lymph nodes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the NALT infection experiments.

claim: The degree of attenuation observed for T7SS mutants was not observed when mice were infected intranasally with a Cor-deficient strain of Mtb (Mtbcor::Tn7).
source: This degree of attenuation was not observed when we infected mice intranasally with a Cor-deficient strain of Mtb (Mtbcor::Tn7) that is also attenuated in vivo (Zacharia et al., 2013; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Zacharia et al., 2013.

claim: The lower CFU recovered from cervical lymph nodes of mice infected with T7SS mutant Mtb strains may be due to reduced translocation across M cells.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the lower CFU recovered from cervical lymph nodes of mice infected with T7SS mutant Mtb strains may be due to reduced translocation across M cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing different Mtb strains.

claim: Human adenoids contain SR-B1+/NKM+ M cells.
source: We first demonstrated that human adenoids contain SR-B1+/NKM+ M cells by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 5D), similar to our observations from mouse NALT (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Approximately 10% of adenoid cells were EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells.
source: We next confirmed the presence of M cells in human adenoids by flow cytometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for gating strategy) and observed that approximately 10% of adenoid cells were EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells, while about 1% of the cells were EpCAM+/NKM+ double positive M cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: About 1% of adenoid cells were EpCAM+/NKM+ double positive M cells.
source: We next confirmed the presence of M cells in human adenoids by flow cytometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for gating strategy) and observed that approximately 10% of adenoid cells were EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells, while about 1% of the cells were EpCAM+/NKM+ double positive M cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Approximately 20% of primary human M cells (marked as EpCAM+/NKM+ cells) were SR-B1 positive.
source: When we analyzed SR-B1 expression using flow cytometry, we observed that approximately 20% of primary human M cells (marked as EpCAM+/NKM+ cells) were SR-B1 positive as compared to less than 2% of the other epithelial cells (EpCAM+/NKM-) (Figure 5F), verifying our observation that SR-B1 is expressed predominately by M cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Less than 2% of other epithelial cells (EpCAM+/NKM-) were SR-B1 positive.
source: When we analyzed SR-B1 expression using flow cytometry, we observed that approximately 20% of primary human M cells (marked as EpCAM+/NKM+ cells) were SR-B1 positive as compared to less than 2% of the other epithelial cells (EpCAM+/NKM-) (Figure 5F), verifying our observation that SR-B1 is expressed predominately by M cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SR-B1 is expressed predominately by M cells in vivo.
source: When we analyzed SR-B1 expression using flow cytometry, we observed that approximately 20% of primary human M cells (marked as EpCAM+/NKM+ cells) were SR-B1 positive as compared to less than 2% of the other epithelial cells (EpCAM+/NKM-) (Figure 5F), verifying our observation that SR-B1 is expressed predominately by M cells in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The number of GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM+ M cells ranged from 0.1–8%.
source: The number of GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM+ M cells ranged from 0.1–8% while we were unable to identify any GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that M cells were a preferred route of entry for Mtb in adenoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: No GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells were identified.
source: The number of GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM+ M cells ranged from 0.1–8% while we were unable to identify any GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that M cells were a preferred route of entry for Mtb in adenoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: M cells were a preferred route of entry for Mtb in adenoids.
source: The number of GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM+ M cells ranged from 0.1–8% while we were unable to identify any GFP+ Mtb containing EpCAM+/NKM- epithelial cells (Figure 5G), suggesting that M cells were a preferred route of entry for Mtb in adenoids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: More GFP+/EpCAM+/NKM+ cells were observed after infection with WT Mtb as compared to Mtb eccD1::Tn.
source: We infected adenoids with GFP+ WT Mtb or GFP+ Mtb eccD1::Tn and observed more GFP+/EpCAM+/NKM+ cells after infection with WT Mtb as compared to Mtb eccD1::Tn (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Mtb can enter via mouse NALT and human adenoid M cells in a T7SS dependent manner.
source: Taken together, we conclude that Mtb can enter via mouse NALT and human adenoid M cells in a T7SS dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data from Figure 5.

claim: M cell transcytosis depends on the Mtb Type VII secretion machine and its major virulence factor EsxA.
source: Here, we show that M cell transcytosis depends on the Mtb Type VII secretion machine and its major virulence factor EsxA.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Scavenger receptor B1 (SR-B1) is an EsxA receptor on airway M cells.
source: We identify scavenger receptor B1 (SR-B1) as an EsxA receptor on airway M cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SR-B1 is required for Mtb binding to and translocation across M cells in mouse and human tissue.
source: SR-B1 is required for Mtb binding to and translocation across M cells in mouse and human tissue.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EsxA has a previously undescribed role in mucosal invasion.
source: Together, our data demonstrate a previously undescribed role for Mtb EsxA in mucosal invasion and identify SR-B1 as the airway M cell receptor for Mtb.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SR-B1 is the airway M cell receptor for Mtb.
source: Together, our data demonstrate a previously undescribed role for Mtb EsxA in mucosal invasion and identify SR-B1 as the airway M cell receptor for Mtb.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EsxA may directly interact with M cell SR-B1 in a cell contact-dependent manner.
source: Thus, EsxA may directly interact with M cell SR-B1 in a cell contact-dependent manner (Conrad et al., 2017), leading to SR-B1 receptor-mediated internalization similar to its function in both hepatitis C virus and Plasmodium vivax uptake (Heo et al., 2006; Manzoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from cited literature.

claim: SR-B1 mediates receptor-mediated internalization in hepatitis C virus uptake.
source: Thus, EsxA may directly interact with M cell SR-B1 in a cell contact-dependent manner (Conrad et al., 2017), leading to SR-B1 receptor-mediated internalization similar to its function in both hepatitis C virus and Plasmodium vivax uptake (Heo et al., 2006; Manzoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heo et al., 2006; Manzoni et al., 2017.

claim: SR-B1 mediates receptor-mediated internalization in Plasmodium vivax uptake.
source: Thus, EsxA may directly interact with M cell SR-B1 in a cell contact-dependent manner (Conrad et al., 2017), leading to SR-B1 receptor-mediated internalization similar to its function in both hepatitis C virus and Plasmodium vivax uptake (Heo et al., 2006; Manzoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heo et al., 2006; Manzoni et al., 2017.

claim: Other host proteins that interact with EsxA include laminin, β2 microglobulin, and TLR-2.
source: Although SR-B1 has not been previously identified as an EsxA receptor, prior studies have found other host proteins that interact with EsxA, including laminin (Kinhikar et al., 2010), β2 microglobulin (Sreejit et al., 2014), and TLR-2 (Pathak et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kinhikar et al., 2010; Sreejit et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2007.

claim: Other receptors could partly compensate for loss of SR-B1 on M cells.

evidence: This is a speculative claim to explain residual binding/translocation in SR-B1 deficient cells.

claim: Mtb may encode for factors other than EsxA that also mediate M cell binding and translocation.

evidence: This is a speculative claim to explain residual binding/translocation in EsxA deficient strains.

claim: T7SS deficient strains of Mtb are attenuated in vivo and in macrophages.
source: A possible alternate interpretation for this result centers on the observation that T7SS deficient strains of Mtb are attenuated in vivo and in macrophages (Stanley et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stanley et al., 2003.

claim: The reduced CFU recovered from cervical lymph nodes of mice infected with T7SS-deficient Mtb is not simply due to an attenuation defect within macrophages.
source: We therefore propose that the reduced CFU recovered from cervical lymph nodes of mice infected with T7SS-deficient Mtb is not simply due to an attenuation defect within macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with the Cor-deficient strain data.

claim: SR-B1 has been well characterized as a high-density lipoprotein receptor involved in cholesterol uptake.
source: SR-B1 has been well characterized as a high-density lipoprotein receptor involved in cholesterol uptake (Acton et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Acton et al., 1996.

claim: SR-B1 binds several bacterial molecules, including lipopolysacharide and lipoteicheic acid.
source: It has also been shown that SR-B1 binds several bacterial molecules, including lipopolysacharide and lipoteicheic acid produced by gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria, respectively (Bocharov et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bocharov et al., 2004.

claim: SR-B1 has been reported as a receptor for mycobacteria, primarily in macrophages.
source: Although direct interaction of EsxA and SR-B1 has not previously been shown, SR-B1 has been reported as a receptor for mycobacteria (Philips et al., 2005; Schäfer et al., 2009), primarily in macrophages (reviewed in Stamm et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Philips et al., 2005; Schäfer et al., 2009; Stamm et al., 2015.

claim: When SR-B1-/- mice were infected with Mtb via the aerosol route, there was no difference in bacterial replication, granuloma size, cytokine secretion, or survival within the first 4 months post-infection compared to wild-type mice.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schäfer et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of M cell SR-B1 should reduce bacterial dissemination from the airway and enhance mouse survival.
source: Based on our current data and previous results showing improved mouse survival during aerosol Mtb infection when M cells are reduced (Nair et al., 2016), we predict that loss of M cell SR-B1 should reduce bacterial dissemination from the airway and enhance mouse survival.
evidence: This is a prediction based on current data and prior citation to Nair et al., 2016.

claim: SR-B1-/- mice experience defective intrauterine and post-natal development and are not born at normal Mendellian ratios.
source: SR-B1-/- mice experience defective intrauterine and post-natal development and as a result are not born at normal Mendellian ratios (Santander et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Santander et al., 2013.

claim: SR-B1-/- mice manifest increased serum HDL, cardiovascular defects and altered adrenal hormones.
source: In addition, they manifest increased serum HDL, cardiovascular defects and altered adrenal hormones (Trigatti et al., 1999), making them incompatible with such a study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trigatti et al., 1999.

claim: Adenoid M cells may serve as a portal of entry for Mtb.
source: Adenoid M cells may serve as a portal of entry for Mtb, with significant implications for Mtb pathogenesis in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from human adenoids.

claim: Respiratory MALT is more abundant in children than adults.
source: Because respiratory MALT is more abundant in children than adults (Tschernig and Pabst, 2000) and M cells are a key component of MALT (Corr et al., 2008), we propose that the increased incidence of extrapulmonary TB in children (Yang et al., 2004) is due to M cell mediated translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tschernig and Pabst, 2000.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Corr et al., 2008.

claim: Many bacterial and viral pathogens use the airway as a portal of entry.
source: Many bacterial and viral pathogens use the airway as a portal of entry, such as P. aeruginosa (Bucior et al., 2012), Bacillus anthracis (Russell et al., 2008), Streptococcus pneumonia (Wilkosz et al., 2012), Streptococcus pyogenes (Barnett et al., 2015), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (Liu et al., 2016) and varicella zoster virus (Messaoudi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: B. abortus uses PrP(C) for M cell mediated translocation.
source: Similarly, a variety of pathogens that invade via the gastrointestinal tract such as B. abortus via PrP(C) (Nakato et al., 2012), S. typhimurium via GP2 (Hase et al., 2009), and murine norovirus (Gonzalez-Hernandez et al., 2014) possibly via CD300lf (Haga et al., 2016; Orchard et al., 2016) use unique receptors for M cell mediated translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakato et al., 2012.

claim: A broad array of airway pathogens exploit distinct M cell receptors to penetrate the airway mucosa and disseminate.

evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the patterns observed with various pathogens.

claim: EsxA and SR-B1 form a molecular synapse required for Mtb translocation across M cells in vitro and in vivo in both mice and humans.
source: Utilizing mouse models and in vitro models, we identify EsxA and SR-B1 as a molecular synapse required for Mtb translocation across M cells in vitro and in vivo in both mice and humans.
